I am currently reading a book called "The Alternative Of Real Ecology" Kveldulf Gunnar Larsson. I disagree with his conclusions, which are fatalistic, but find he really nails one issue: there is a difference between environmentalism and conservationism.

Environmentalism insists that we can avoid changing the qualitative problem with humanity, namely too many people consuming too much stuff, by adding regulatory factors on top, like "green" EnergyStar compliant appliances, carbon caps and taxes, and limits on consumption. It misses the point that for every one person who complies, someone else will not, which means the compliers put themselves at a disadvantage and the non-compliers win, making it a classical suicidal policy. Even more, however, until we change the basic structure of society from endless growth to support a consumer economy and the fiction of the necessity of massive personal choice in products, humanity will simply serve as an agent for consumption of nature for the production of landfill. Conservationism on the other hand suggests that we set aside vast amounts of land as a means of both preserving it and regulating human growth; this parallels both National Socialist policy and aristocracy, which gave vast hunting preserves to aristocrats so that these would be preserved from extensive human intervention.

With that in mind, the first step would be to translate the issue from "environmentalism" -- which as you correctly note is framed by the Left -- into a question of regulating human population, with the obvious Darwinian corollary that we should be producing better (more intelligent, more moral and healthier/more beautiful) human beings instead of an endless flood of lumpenproles who crave fast food and iPhones.

At this point, the issue can be tied in to conservatism in general. While few identity as conservatives on the Alt Right because of the disgraceful behavior of mainstream conservatives, technically any Rightist views fall under conservatism: we aim to conserve humanity at its best, which means conservative policies for society and values for the individual. Conservatives are also inherently conservationists, although the Left has done its best to hide that fact. This gives us a string of things to conserve: race, culture, nature, religion, sanctity, honor, pride, and the transcendentals, "the good, the beautiful and the true."

European-descended people have been birthing new kids at or below replacement rates, so among our people, growth is not a problem. That does not answer the question of worldwide numbers, and we consume more resources per capita than a third world nation, but at the same time avoid engaging in some of the most destructive behaviors in the third world (tire fires, slash 'n burn agriculture, dumping of toxic waste and old technology). This means we face the worst of all dilemmas, a complex one. It would make sense to balance the equation by reducing our consumer consumption and sending home those who are not of the founding group of the nation, which would reduce consumption to compensate for the new births.

Zooming out a bit, there is no way the overpopulation problem can be avoided, and a crash is coming. We have approximately 7.5bn humans, and while we could store them all in Texas, the main factors are that for every person, a corresponding amount of infrastructure must be built, and every person on earth wants a Western-style large suburban house, two cars, big fridge and wide screen television. With that in mind, we need to face that fact that not everyone can have this lifestyle and perhaps we should limit it to those of higher intelligence who are less likely to be abusive and buy tons of gadgets to throw out or drive giant engine cars. Although there are no technological solutions, technology can help mediate this problem if we focus on making consumer appliances last longer, so that less waste is produced, and through cultural change, deprecate certain wasteful behaviors. If we could convince most people to stop smoking, we can encourage them to stop driving giant cars, buying too much stuff, wasting food and otherwise over-consuming.

At the end of the day, however, we face a choice. Either we damage our prospects and let the rest of the world ride free, or we assert our self-interest and live according to what we can provide for ourselves, and compensate for the damage done by conserving large swathes of forest to absorb the pollution and renew natural cycles. This would require a system more assertive than democracy, at which point we could do things like limit who owns cars and how much driving people do, stop wasteful products from being sold on a case-by-case basis (case-by-case thinking is one of the foundations of conservative thought; rules are for insects), and design smaller cities instead of megaplexes. This suggests that our most ethical action is not to commit suicide, but to change our behavior.
